The claimed lift mechanism is attributed to a Thomas Townsend Brown patent of the late 1950s or early 1960s; the board's own record of both Brown patents is that neither claims anti-gravity. Eric Davis, from inside the classification line, says no such craft exists. Every claimant on this thread runs into this node, which is the point of it.

dossier.narrative: The argument for a node with no evidence behind it is that the alternative is worse. Before this build the board carried Steven Greer, the Disclosure Project, the Brown patents and the contractor estate, and carried nothing for the object all of them are talking about. A reader could not see that the ARV is a single claim with many carriers, because the carriers were joined to each other and to institutions, never to the thing itself. Building the hub makes the shape legible and, more usefully, makes the shape falsifiable: every edge into it is dated, typed and tiered, so the reader can count how much of the convergence is documented. The answer here is: very little. The strongest artefact is a working file an Aviation Week editor never published, and inside it the witness refuses to stand behind his own figures and disowns part of the drawing made from his account. The sizes then grow more precise with each retelling, which is the opposite of what happens to a measurement. The claimed lift mechanism is attributed to a Thomas Townsend Brown patent, and the board's own record is that neither Brown patent claims anti-gravity: both claim thrust by electrical fields in a dielectric medium. That join is the reason this thread belongs to a board about defense contractors at all, and it is also the reason it does not support what it is usually cited to support.
openQuestions: The Aviation Week and Space Technology issue of 1 October 1990, which the 1990 notes name as carrying McCandlish's two paintings. It is the only element of this thread published in the contemporary trade press and nobody has opened it.
The McCandlish cut-away drawing itself, as printed in the Disclosure Project Briefing Document's plate section, which this session did not extract.
Whether any record of Brad Sorensen exists under that surname. The 1990 document gives a first name, a school, a client list and an hourly rate, and nobody in the opened record appears to have tried.
dossier.whatItIs: A claimed saucer-shaped craft, called the Alien Reproduction Vehicle and the Flux Liner, said to have been shown in a hangar at Norton Air Force Base on 12 November 1988. No record of its existence has been opened. The whole account descends from one second-hand relay: an industrial designer said he saw three such craft, and an aerospace illustrator who was not present drew them from that verbal description. Two primary documents carry the description, William B. Scott's unpublished 1990 interview notes and the Disclosure Project's April 2001 Briefing Document, and they are why this node exists, not evidence that the craft does.
dossier.whyImplicated: It is on this map as the worked example of a rule the board adopted on 18 September 2026: the thing claimed about is a node in its own right, and it is the hub every claimant runs into. Ten people arguing about a place, joined only to each other, hide the convergence; joined to the place, they show it. This is the first craft node the board has ever carried, and its edges are deliberately mixed: the sole eyewitness, the illustrator who drew it, the trade-press editor who investigated and never published, the anonymous site that sells reconstructions of it, and a government scientist who says it never existed. Its degree means a lot is claimed here. It does not mean any of it is true, and the tier on each edge says which is which.
